notes: PitchIQ training drill library, version 2 (soccer/coaching/drills.py validates it; DESIGN v2 section 7). Fourteen drills across the seven playing levels. Every drill is a PitchIQ adaptation or a PitchIQ original session, labelled so in source_reference with the ids of the coaching sources that informed it (see soccer/coaching/sources.json); none is a verbatim federation session and no federation reviewed or endorses PitchIQ. Field sizes, durations, player counts and physical loads are PitchIQ starting points (origin PITCHIQ-PROPOSAL, unvalidated) to adapt to the players. No drill contains heading. A drill is recommended only for a finding of one of its related_tactical_detector values; success_signals_next_match name the measured relation the next match should show in more of its situations, and the report fills in its own numbers. Plain ASCII only (the PDF writer uses base-14 Helvetica). player_count counts every player a drill uses, goalkeepers included: "N v M with goalkeepers" is N + M outfield players and two keepers. recommended_format lists the match formats whose squad can play the drill as written: a team of a larger format may play it as a smaller game, a team of a smaller format is never offered it, and a drill offered below 11v11 uses relative role words (wide defender, central midfielder, central defender), not 11v11 role names. Every success signal ends with "in more of these moments than in this match"; the report leaves that comparison out when this match did not judge the check. No drill text uses a repetition word the report refuses under 3 minutes of play (repeat, pattern, often).

drills.name: 2v2 Help Your Teammate

player_count.note: 2 v 2 on one or more small pitches; extra pairs wait beside the pitch and swap in every round.

equipment: One ball per pitch and spares

field_setup.notes: A small pitch with a small goal at each end and a helper line about 5 m in front of each goal. Make the pitch smaller for the youngest groups and larger as the players grow.

duration.blocks: 4 rounds of 2 min with a 1 min drink and talk break

instructions: Play 2 v 2 to small goals. When your team does not have the ball, one player goes to the ball and the other player is the helper.
The helper stays between the helper line and the goal until the ball is back with the team.
When your team has the ball, the player without it stays a few steps behind the ball, ready to help and to protect our goal.
There is no tackling or sliding in this game: defenders block the way to goal and poke the ball away when it is loose.
Swap jobs every round so every player tries both: going to the ball and helping.
The coach restarts with a new ball after each goal, so everybody plays a lot.
coaching_points: Who is closest to the ball? That player goes to the ball quickly and slows down when close.
Helper: stand between the ball and our goal, where you can see the ball and the goal.
Helper: not too close to your teammate, so you are ready if the dribbler gets past.
Praise effort and good choices; keep the words short and simple.
progression: Remove the helper line so the players decide where to help from.
Make the pitch a little bigger so the helper has to judge the distance.
Play 3 v 3: one helper and two players near the ball.
regression: Play 1 v 1 to a goal first, then add the helper.
Make the pitch smaller so the helper stays close to the goal.
Walk with the ball for the first round.

success_signals_next_match.text: When the other team has the ball in our half, someone goes to the ball in more of these moments than in this match.
When we have the ball, someone is ready to protect our goal in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the FA swift support game for 7-11s (one player goes to the ball, a teammate guards a line in front of goal); not a verbatim federation session.
PitchIQ adaptation; the two jobs follow the FA pressing and covering programme for 7-11s.

drills.name: 4v4 Spread Out: Tall, Wide, Deep

player_count.note: 4 v 4 on one pitch; with more players run two pitches side by side.

equipment: Flat markers for the pitch and three lanes

field_setup.notes: Two small goals on each end line, one near each corner, so each team attacks two goals. Mark three lanes along the pitch with flat markers for the first rounds.

duration.blocks: 4 rounds of 3 min with a 1 min break

instructions: Play 4 v 4 without goalkeepers; each team attacks two small goals and defends two.
When your team has the ball, take one job each: one player tall (nearest the goals you attack), two players wide (one near each side line) and one player deep (behind the ball).
In the first rounds a goal counts double when the scoring team had a player in each of the three lanes.
Swap jobs every round so each player tries tall, wide and deep.
The coach restarts with a new ball after every goal.
coaching_points: Make the pitch big when we have the ball: tall, wide and deep.
Look up: where is the space with nobody in it?
Wide players stay near the side line until the ball comes their way.
Deep player: stay behind the ball so the dribbler can play it back to you.
progression: Remove the lanes and the bonus; the players find the shape on their own.
Play 5 v 5 with a goalkeeper for each team, still tall, wide and deep.
regression: Play 3 v 3 with three jobs: tall, wide and deep.
Walk the shape first without opponents, then add them.

success_signals_next_match.text: When we have the ball, the players use the field from one side to the other in more of these moments than in this match.
When we have the ball, the team is spread from deep to tall in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: Inspired by the U.S. Soccer 4v4 1-2-1 diamond, where each player carries height, width or depth; PitchIQ adaptation, not a verbatim federation session.
The four-goal game idea comes from the Canada Soccer grassroots game examples; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: Go to the Ball Corridor Game

player_count.note: 1 v 1 in each corridor, then 2 v 2 across two joined corridors; the others queue and rotate.

field_setup.notes: Long thin corridors about 8 m wide side by side, each with a start line and an end line. The attacker scores by dribbling over the far end line and stopping the ball there.

duration.blocks: 6 rounds of 1 min with 1 min rest

instructions: The attacker starts at one end with the ball; the defender starts at the other end, facing them.
On the coach's call the defender goes quickly to the ball, slows down when close and tries to stop the attacker from reaching the end line.
The defender gets a point for stopping the attacker or for poking the ball out of the corridor; there is no tackling or sliding.
Swap roles every round so everybody attacks and defends.
Then join two corridors and play 2 v 2: the player nearest the ball goes to it and the other one helps.
coaching_points: Go to the ball quickly, then take small steps when you get close.
Stand a little sideways with bent knees, ready to move.
Watch the ball and try to make the dribbler slow down or go sideways.
progression: Start the defender further away, so they have to arrive quickly.
Make the corridor wider, so the attacker has more room to get past.
regression: The attacker walks with the ball in the first round.
Make the corridor narrower, so the defender has less space to look after.

success_signals_next_match.text: When the other team has the ball in our half, the nearest player goes to the ball in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the corridor game in the FA practising the press session (week one of the 7-11s programme); not a verbatim federation session.

drills.name: 3v2 Pressure and Cover

player_count.note: 3 attackers v 2 defenders; extra players wait in pairs and swap in after each attack.

equipment: Two small goals or cone gates

field_setup.notes: The defenders guard two small goals or cone gates on one end line; the attackers start from the other end line. Mark a cover line about 6 m in front of the goals for the first rounds.

duration.blocks: 5 rounds of 2 min with 1 min rest and questions

instructions: Three attackers play against two defenders toward the defenders' goals; each attack starts with a ball from the coach.
The defender nearest the ball gives pressure: goes to the ball, slows down and stops the dribbler from going forward.
The second defender gives cover: behind and to the side of the first defender, between the ball and the goal.
If the defenders get the ball, they score by dribbling over the far end line.
There is no tackling in this game: defenders block the way, poke the ball away or intercept it.
Swap the defenders after every two attacks so everybody defends.
coaching_points: Pressure: the closest defender goes, slows down and stands side-on.
Cover: behind the first defender at an angle, close enough to help and far enough to see the ball and the goal.
When the ball moves the jobs can change: the new closest player gives pressure and the other one covers.
Ask the players: who gave pressure, who gave cover, and where did the cover stand?
progression: Remove the cover line and let the defenders find the cover position.
Add a third defender who starts a few seconds late from behind the attackers.
Widen the pitch so the cover player has to move across as the ball moves.
regression: Play 2 v 1 with the cover line in front of the goals.
The attackers walk with the ball in the first round.
Narrow the pitch so the cover position is easier to find.

success_signals_next_match.text: When a defender goes to the ball, a teammate gives cover behind in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball in our third, someone gives pressure in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the FA swift support session for 7-11s (one player presses while a teammate covers); not a verbatim federation session.
The approach cues (side-on, slow down when close) follow the FA practising the press session; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 4v4 Someone Stays Back

player_count.note: 4 v 4 with or without goalkeepers; extra players rotate in every round.

equipment: Two goals (small goals, or goals with goalkeepers)

field_setup.notes: Mark a safety line across the pitch about 8 m in front of each goal.

duration.blocks: 4 rounds of 3 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Play 4 v 4 to goals. When your team has the ball, at least one player stays behind the ball in your own half, ready to protect your goal.
A goal does not count if the scoring team had nobody behind the ball when the shot was taken.
Anyone can be the player who stays back: when a back player dribbles forward, a teammate takes the place behind.
When the other team has the ball, one player guards the safety line in front of your goal while the others defend.
Rotate so everyone has a turn as the player who stays back.
coaching_points: Before you join the attack, look back: is someone staying behind the ball?
If a teammate dribbles forward from the back, take their place behind the ball.
The player who stays back stands in the middle, behind the ball, where they can reach either side.
Staying back is a job, not a punishment: praise the player who does it well.
progression: Remove the safety line and let the players judge where to stay.
Give the defending team a bonus point for a quick attack that starts while the other team has nobody behind the ball.
Play 5 v 5 with goalkeepers and keep one player behind the ball at all times when attacking.
regression: Name the player who stays back for each round instead of letting the players decide.
Make the pitch shorter so the player who stays back is closer to the play.

success_signals_next_match.text: When we have the ball beyond our own third, someone stays behind the ball in more of these moments than in this match.
When a back player moves forward, a teammate fills the space behind in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the England supporting on the line session (one player keeps a line in front of goal; the page states no age); not a verbatim federation session.
In the U.S. Soccer 7v7 1-3-2-1 the back players also support the attack; PitchIQ adds the stay-back job.

drills.name: 5v4 Defensive Recovery

player_count.note: 5 attackers v 4 defenders, plus a goalkeeper if available; extra players rotate in as the defender who recovers.

equipment: Flat markers and two start cones

field_setup.notes: About half of a 9v9 pitch: a goal with a goalkeeper on one end line and two small target goals on the far line. Two start cones about 10 m behind the play mark where the recovering defender starts.

duration.blocks: 4 blocks of 3 min with 1 to 2 min rest; feedback in the rests

instructions: Five attackers attack the goal against three defenders in place and one defender who starts from a cone behind the play.
On the coach's call the recovering defender runs back by the shortest route to get between the ball and the goal.
The defenders in place delay: the nearest one gives pressure, the next one covers, and the others stay compact in front of the goal until the recovering defender arrives.
If the defenders get the ball, they score by dribbling or playing it into a small target goal.
Start the recovering defender from different cones so the route back changes.
The ball is in play in every repetition; avoid plain running without the ball.
coaching_points: Recover by the shortest route toward your own goal, then look up to find the ball.
Delay first: the nearest defender slows the attack while teammates get into position.
Cover at an angle behind the first defender, not too close to them.
Keep the gaps between defenders small on the ball side; the far side can be wider.
Ask: where could you have stood to help if the attack had come to your side?
progression: Start the recovering defender further away or later.
Play 6 v 5 with two recovering defenders starting from different cones.
Add a second, wider target for the attackers so the back players have to shift across together.
regression: Play 4 v 3 with the recovering defender starting closer.
Limit the attackers to three touches each so the defenders have more time.

success_signals_next_match.text: When the other team has the ball in our half, cover behind the nearest defender is there in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, our players get goal-side of the ball in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, the ball-side gaps between our back players stay small in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation built on the England description of covering and recovering (shortest route back, between ball and goal); not a verbatim federation session.
Delay and recover ideas from the England cover and recover session for 12-16s; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 9v9 Wide and Deep Shape

player_count.note: Two teams of 7 to 9 with goalkeepers; with fewer players play 7 v 7 with the same jobs.

equipment: Flat markers for three lanes and the thirds

field_setup.notes: Use the team's normal 9v9 pitch, marked into three lanes along its length and split into thirds.

duration.blocks: Shadow play 4 min, then 3 game blocks of 4 min with 1 to 2 min rest

instructions: Shadow play: the team moves the ball through its 1-3-2-3 shape without opponents; at every change of direction everyone adjusts to stay tall, wide and deep.
Game: 9 v 9. When your team has the ball, keep at least one player in each lane and players in at least two of the thirds.
When a back player moves forward with the ball, a teammate fills the space behind in that lane.
A goal counts double when the scoring team had a player in all three lanes.
Rotate positions between blocks so the players learn the jobs of the back block and the front block.
coaching_points: Width: the wide players hold their lane until the ball comes their way.
Depth: someone stays behind the ball to support and to protect the goal.
Height: the player furthest forward keeps the opponents deep.
When a back player goes forward, who fills the space behind? Agree it before the block starts.
progression: Remove the lanes so the players judge the width on their own.
Limit the touches of the team with the ball so it has to find the open lane quickly.
regression: Play 7 v 7 with jobs given by the coach.
Make the shadow play longer and add one passive defender at a time.

success_signals_next_match.text: When we have the ball, the left, the middle and the right are all used in more of these moments than in this match.
When we have the ball, the team is spread from deep to tall in more of these moments than in this match.
When a wide defender moves forward, the space behind in that lane is filled in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: Inspired by the U.S. Soccer 9v9 1-3-2-3 (two blocks of four); PitchIQ adaptation, not a verbatim federation session.

drills.name: 6v6 Defensive Unit Coordination

player_count.note: 6 v 6 plus goalkeepers on half of an 11v11 pitch; extra players rotate in every block.

field_setup.notes: Half of an 11v11 pitch split into three channels along its length. Each team has a back group of three and a front group of three.

duration.blocks: 4 blocks of 4 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Play 6 v 6 with goalkeepers; each team sets up with three at the back and three in front.
A wide back player may join the attack only when the nearest central back has moved across toward that side and one teammate holds behind the ball.
If the defending team gets the ball while the attacking team has fewer than two players behind it, a goal from that move counts double.
When the ball goes wide, the defending back group shifts across together and keeps the middle protected.
Swap roles between blocks so each player has a turn as the wide back player.
coaching_points: Before the wide back goes forward: who covers the space behind, and who holds behind the ball?
Central back: move across toward the ball side as the wide back advances.
Protect the middle first, then shift across as a unit when the ball goes wide.
Near enough to step in, far enough apart to support each other: keep the gaps small on the ball side.
progression: Remove the condition and let the players decide when the wide back can go.
Add a neutral player for the team with the ball, so the defenders are outnumbered.
Widen the pitch to make the shift across longer.
regression: Play 4 v 4 plus goalkeepers with one wide back and one central back per team.
Walk through the shift and the cover once without opponents before each block.

success_signals_next_match.text: When a wide defender advances, the channel behind is covered in more of these moments than in this match.
When we have the ball beyond our own third, enough players stay behind the ball in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, the ball-side gaps in our back line stay small in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation drawing on the England press and cover programme for 12-16s (protect the middle, shift across as a unit); not a verbatim federation session.
Built around the U.S. Soccer U13-U14 attacking principle of keeping a defensive shape behind the ball; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 3v3 Cover the Line

player_count.note: 3 v 3, or 2 v 2 to start, on parallel small pitches; rotate teams every round.

field_setup.notes: Parallel pitches about 18 x 14 m with a covering line about 9 m in front of each end line. A team scores by dribbling over the other team's end line.

duration.blocks: 5 rounds of 2 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Play 3 v 3; a team scores by dribbling over the other team's end line.
The team without the ball keeps one player on or behind its covering line at all times.
One defender presses the ball at an angle, the second covers behind, and the third stays goal-side on the side away from the ball, ready for a switch.
Rotate who guards the covering line after every goal.
coaching_points: One presses, one covers: two defenders do not go to the ball at the same time.
Press at an angle to steer the attacker toward the side line.
The far-side defender stays goal-side of the ball in the half away from it, so a switch can be met.
As the ball moves the jobs change: the new nearest player presses and the others adjust.
progression: Remove the covering line condition.
Make the pitch wider so the far-side job matters more.
Add a time limit for the defending team to stop the attack.
regression: Play 2 v 2 with one presser and one cover on the line.
Make the pitch narrower so the cover distance is shorter.

success_signals_next_match.text: When our nearest defender presses, a teammate covers behind in more of these moments than in this match.
When the ball is wide, someone protects the far side goal-side of the ball in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the cover the line game in the England cover and recover session for 12-16s; not a verbatim federation session.
The covering line also appears in the England supporting on the line session; PitchIQ adaptation.
The press, cover and far-side jobs follow the England press, cover and balance session for 12-16s; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 8v8 Transition and Cover

player_count.note: 8 v 8 with goalkeepers; with more players add up to four neutral players who join the team with the ball.

field_setup.notes: About two thirds of an 11v11 pitch with three channels marked along its length. Spare balls at the sides for quick restarts.

duration.blocks: 4 blocks of 5 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Play 8 v 8 with goalkeepers; each team defends with a back line of three or four, with a wide defender on each side.
Wide defenders are encouraged to advance with the ball, but the team keeps at least two outfield players behind the ball whenever it is in the final third.
When a wide defender advances, a central midfielder drops or the nearest central defender shifts across to cover the channel behind.
If the ball changes team while the attacking side had fewer than two players behind it, a goal from that move counts double.
After each goal the coach restarts with a ball to the team that conceded, so the switch of jobs is quick.
coaching_points: Plan the cover while you attack, in case the ball changes team: who looks after the advanced wide defender's channel?
Central midfielder: drop toward the back line on the side the wide defender left.
Nearest central defender: shift toward the touchline as the wide defender advances.
A teammate taking the wide defender's place is a valid answer too: name it when you see it.
progression: Add four neutral players who play for the team with the ball, so the defending team is outnumbered.
A goal scored within five seconds of the ball changing team counts double.
regression: Play 6 v 6 with one wide defender per team.
Freeze play when a wide defender advances and ask who covers before restarting.

success_signals_next_match.text: When a wide defender advances, the channel behind is covered by a teammate in more of these moments than in this match.
When we have the ball in the final third, enough players stay behind the ball in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the England read and react session for 12-16s (5v5 plus four neutral players, quick goals after the ball changes team score more); not a verbatim federation session.
The U.S. Soccer U15-U16 game model asks for a defensive shape behind the ball while attacking; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 8v8 Shift Across Nine Zones

player_count.note: 8 v 8 with goalkeepers; with fewer players, 6 v 6 on a smaller pitch.

equipment: Flat markers to divide the pitch into nine zones

field_setup.notes: Divide the pitch into nine zones: three channels across and three thirds along. The zone lines help players see the ball side and the far side.

duration.blocks: 4 blocks of 5 min with 1 to 2 min rest

instructions: Play 8 v 8. When the defending team stops an attack and scores from that move, the goal is worth the number of its players who were in the zone where it got the ball.
When the ball is in a wide channel, the defending team keeps at least one player goal-side of the ball in the far half.
The back line shifts across with the ball and keeps the gaps on the ball side small.
The nearest player presses the ball and a teammate covers behind.
The coach freezes play now and then to check the ball side, the far side and the cover.
coaching_points: Shift as a unit toward the ball; protect the middle first.
Far side: stay goal-side and inside, close enough to meet a switch of play.
Ball side: keep the gaps between the back players small, especially with an opponent between them.
Pressing all game is not possible: when the press is off, delay and keep the shape.
progression: Lock players into their thirds so the shift has to happen as a unit.
Give the attacking team a floating player.
regression: Play 6 v 6 on a smaller pitch.
Shadow the shift first: the coach moves the ball by hand and the team adjusts.

success_signals_next_match.text: When the ball is in a wide channel, a defender is goal-side in the far half in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, the ball-side gaps in our back line stay small in more of these moments than in this match.
When the nearest defender presses, cover behind is there in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ adaptation of the nine-zone game in the England pressing zones session for 12-16s; not a verbatim federation session.
Ball-side and far-side jobs from the England press, cover and balance session for 12-16s; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 9v9 Rest-Defence Structure

player_count.note: 9 v 9 with goalkeepers; with 18 players use 8 v 8 plus goalkeepers.

field_setup.notes: About three quarters of an 11v11 pitch. Mark a line across the end of each team's defensive third.

duration.blocks: Walk-through 5 min, then 4 blocks of 4 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Rest defence is a PitchIQ term here: the players who stay behind the ball while the team attacks, counted against the opponents' forwards who stay up.
Each team attacks with a rest-defence group of at least two outfield players behind the ball, taken from the back line and the central midfielders.
The defending team leaves two forwards up; the rest-defence group keeps at least one more player behind the ball than those forwards.
If the defending team gets the ball and scores within ten seconds, the goal counts double.
The coach can freeze an attack to check the rest-defence group: who is in it, where they stand and which channel is open.
coaching_points: The central midfielders and the back line agree the rest-defence group before the wide defenders go forward.
Stay compact behind the ball and close to the forwards left up, so a quick ball forward can be stopped.
When a wide defender advances, the nearest central defender moves across or a midfielder drops into that channel.
Judge it against the plan: a team that attacks with more players accepts fewer behind; agree the number for each match.
progression: The defending team leaves three forwards up, so the rest-defence group has to grow.
Add a target player for the defending team on the halfway line.
regression: Name the rest-defence group for each block.
Play 7 v 7 with one forward left up.

success_signals_next_match.text: When we attack, the players behind the ball outnumber the opponents' forwards left up in more of these moments than in this match.
When a wide defender advances, the channel behind is covered in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ original session, informed by the U.S. Soccer U17+ game model idea of preparing a defensive shape behind the ball while attacking.
The jobs (who presses, who covers, who stays back) follow the England defending roles and responsibilities article; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: Block Compactness: Shadow to 8v8

player_count.note: Eleven players against a coach-moved ball first, then 8 v 8 with goalkeepers; with fewer players, 7 v 7.

equipment: Flat markers for thirds and channels

field_setup.notes: Most of an 11v11 pitch marked in thirds and three channels. In the shadow phase the coach places a ball by hand to set each picture.

duration.blocks: Shadow phase 7 min, then 3 game blocks of 5 min with 1 min rest

instructions: Shadow phase: on the coach's call the team sets a low, mid or high block and moves as the coach places the ball.
On every move the player nearest the ball steps out, the next ones cover, and the far side tucks in.
Game phase: 8 v 8. The defending team scores a bonus point when it stops an attack while its back line is level and close to the midfield line.
Change the block height between blocks so the team practises each one.
coaching_points: Short distances between the lines; the back line moves up and down together.
A compact block accepts space out wide: protect the middle and shift when the ball goes wide.
Far side: tuck in toward the middle but stay ready for a switch of play.
Block height is a plan, not a verdict: agree when to step up and when to drop.
progression: Give the attacking team a floating player in the middle third.
Add a target on each wing so the attacking team can switch play quickly.
regression: Run the shadow phase again with the coach calling out each picture.
Play 7 v 7 on a narrower pitch.

success_signals_next_match.text: When the other team has the ball, the gap between the back line and midfield stays within range in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, the back line is level in more of these moments than in this match.
When the ball is wide, the far side is protected goal-side in more of these moments than in this match.
When the nearest player steps out to the ball, cover behind is there in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: Inspired by the England description of game phases with low, mid and high blocks; PitchIQ adaptation, not a verbatim federation session.
Step out, cover and far-side jobs from the England defending roles article (senior-team inspired); PitchIQ adaptation.
That a compact block accepts space out wide comes from the England article on defending wide areas; PitchIQ adaptation.

drills.name: 11v11 Tactical Phase Training

player_count.note: 11 v 11 when the squad allows; otherwise 11 v 7 phase play with the coach starting each phase.

equipment: Full pitch with flat markers for the channels
Video clips or notes from the last match

field_setup.notes: Full pitch. Each phase restarts from agreed positions so every rehearsal begins from the same picture.

duration.blocks: 3 phases of 8 min with 2 min reviews

instructions: Phase one: build up and attack in the agreed shape against seven defenders; the full-backs advance and the agreed rest-defence group stays behind the ball.
Phase two: the coach plays a new ball to the defending side the moment an attack ends, and the attacking side re-forms its block.
Phase three: 11 v 11 to the match plan; the coach freezes play to review the spacing between the holding midfielder and the near central back.
Choose the phase that starts each block from the analysis of the team's last match.
coaching_points: Agree the rest-defence numbers for the declared style: a possession plan may leave fewer behind than a plan built on quick breaks.
Rotations are welcome when the vacated slot is filled; name who fills it.
Keep the holding midfielder and the near central back close together when a full-back has gone.
Show clips from the last match to set the picture the team wants.
progression: Rehearse against the next opponent's usual shape from the match analysis.
Start phases from awkward pictures, for example both full-backs high.
regression: Walk each phase first without opponents.
Use 11 v 7 for every phase until the shape holds.

success_signals_next_match.text: When we attack, the rest-defence margin (a PitchIQ measure) is positive in more of these moments than in this match.
When a full-back advances, the vacated channel is covered in more of these moments than in this match.
When the other team has the ball, the gap between the back line and midfield stays within range in more of these moments than in this match.

source_reference.note: PitchIQ original session, informed by the match-plan and match-analysis competences in the course description; no course content is reproduced.
The U.S. Soccer U17+ game model idea of a defensive shape behind the ball while attacking; PitchIQ adaptation.
